questions.prompt: A query returns most rows of a small table. Why may the planner choose a sequential scan despite an index?

choices.text: The index is necessarily corrupt whenever it is unused.
The index is ignored because SELECT must name its indexed column first.
Sequential scans are compulsory whenever the query returns more than one row.
Sequential scanning can cost less than using that index.

questions.explanation: An index is an available access path, not a mandate. Reading much of a small table can favor a sequential scan.

sources.title: Introduction to Indexes
sources.claim: Indexes can accelerate finding selected rows but add storage and maintenance overhead; the planner decides whether an index or a sequential scan is economical.

questions.prompt: An endpoint often searches a large table for one selective key. What is the principal benefit of an appropriate index?

choices.text: It guarantees the endpoint will never wait for a transaction lock.
It ensures all qualifying rows are returned in insertion order without ORDER BY.
It can reduce the work needed to locate qualifying rows.
It eliminates the need to check the query predicate.

questions.explanation: An index narrows access to relevant rows. Locking and application response caching remain separate concerns.

sources.title: Introduction to Indexes
sources.claim: Indexes can accelerate finding selected rows but add storage and maintenance overhead; the planner decides whether an index or a sequential scan is economical.

questions.prompt: A B-tree index is on (tenant_id, created_at). Which query best aligns with its leading-column range access?

choices.text: Filter created_at but assume column order never matters.
Filter created_at by a range while assuming tenant_id cannot affect scan work.
Filter tenant_id by a broad range while assuming later dates always narrow every scan equally.
Filter tenant_id by equality and created_at by a date range.

questions.explanation: A leading tenant equality and following date range bound the relevant index span. Column order matters to this access pattern.

sources.title: Multicolumn Indexes
sources.claim: Multicolumn B-tree scans are most efficient with leading-column constraints; leading equalities and the first inequality constrain the scanned range, while later constraints and skip scans can still matter.

questions.prompt: A query constrains only the second column of a two-column PostgreSQL 18+ B-tree index. Which claim is sound?

choices.text: The index is always as efficient as constraining both columns.
It is automatically equivalent to a separate index on that second column.
The index can never participate in any plan for that query.
Usefulness depends on costs and possible skip-scan opportunities.

questions.explanation: Later-column predicates can still be used; favorable distinct-value counts may support skip scans. Avoid universal claims.

sources.title: Multicolumn Indexes
sources.claim: Multicolumn B-tree scans are most efficient with leading-column constraints; leading equalities and the first inequality constrain the scanned range, while later constraints and skip scans can still matter.

questions.prompt: A write-heavy table accumulates many redundant indexes. What tradeoff should a review consider?

choices.text: Removing a redundant index always changes SQL query result semantics.
Indexes are maintained only when a SELECT first requests them.
Each additional index speeds every INSERT by avoiding row validation.
Indexes need storage and must be maintained as data changes.

questions.explanation: Read access gains carry write and storage costs. Review workload evidence before retaining redundant indexes.

sources.title: Introduction to Indexes
sources.claim: Indexes require storage and add overhead to insertion, updating and deletion; they should be used sensibly.

questions.prompt: What materially changes when EXPLAIN ANALYZE is used instead of plain EXPLAIN?

choices.text: The statement executes and actual timing and row counts are reported.
The statement is only planned, so an UPDATE cannot modify any rows.
Only actual results are reported, so estimates cannot be compared with them.
All cost estimates become guaranteed wall-clock milliseconds.

questions.explanation: ANALYZE runs the statement. This matters for expensive queries and data-modifying statements as well as read-only plans.

sources.title: Using EXPLAIN
sources.claim: EXPLAIN shows a planner-selected tree with estimated costs and row counts; EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the statement and reports actual measurements, which can be compared with estimates.

questions.prompt: Which access-path statements are accurate? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Creating an index guarantees all future queries become faster.
Every WHERE predicate requires a separate index to be executable.
An index can reduce work for a selective lookup.
A sequential scan always proves an index definition is invalid.
The planner can prefer a sequential scan when many rows qualify.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect: benefit depends on workload and costs. B: Incorrect: queries also work without such indexes. C: Correct: it provides selective access. D: Incorrect: a scan can be the economical plan. E: Correct: broad retrieval can favor scanning.

sources.title: Introduction to Indexes
sources.claim: Indexes can speed selected-row retrieval, but sensible use depends on access costs and index maintenance overhead.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL 18+, which multicolumn B-tree claims are accurate? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Leading equality conditions can restrict the scanned range.
A condition on a later column is forbidden in an index plan.
A later-column condition can still be checked using the index.
PostgreSQL may use a skip scan when the data distribution favors it.
Column order never influences the amount of index scanning.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: equalities narrow the relevant span. B: Incorrect: later constraints are usable. C: Correct: they can filter index entries. D: Correct: skip scans can avoid scanning irrelevant groups. E: Incorrect: leading constraints generally matter.

sources.title: Multicolumn Indexes
sources.claim: Leading equality constraints and the first inequality restrict B-tree scanning; later conditions can be checked and suitable distributions can enable skip scanning.

questions.prompt: Which costs belong in an index design decision? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Tradeoffs between read benefit and write overhead.
Guaranteed reduction in every query execution time.
Automatic removal of every table-scan plan after the first index is created.
Maintenance work when indexed data changes.
Additional storage for the index structure.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: useful read paths must justify their costs. B: Incorrect: benefits depend on the workload. C: Incorrect: the planner can still prefer a scan. D: Correct: modifications can require maintenance. E: Correct: indexes occupy storage.

sources.title: Introduction to Indexes
sources.claim: Indexes consume storage and increase data-modification overhead, requiring sensible selection.

questions.prompt: Which plan-analysis statements are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: ANALYZE reports measurements from executing the statement.
A large estimated-versus-actual row gap can reveal poor estimates.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE has no effects even for an UPDATE statement.
Planner cost units are guaranteed to equal elapsed milliseconds.
Plain EXPLAIN executes the query and returns actual row counts.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: ANALYZE collects actual execution evidence. B: Correct: compare estimates with observed cardinality. C: Incorrect: the statement executes, including modifications. D: Incorrect: planner costs use internal cost units. E: Incorrect: ordinary EXPLAIN reports an estimated plan.

sources.title: Using EXPLAIN
sources.claim: EXPLAIN shows a planner-selected tree with estimated costs and row counts; EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the statement and reports actual measurements, which can be compared with estimates.
